doc.title: Scott Jimmy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First time singing: valet for tap dancers, and Lester Young
summary: Valeting for Lem Neal and Dickie Sims, he sang Talk of the Town on a gig and was told by Lester Young to go back to the dressing room.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Before – so you’re going to all these live shows with the big bands, Earl Hines and Lunceford. Where did you begin to build up your chops? When did you start to sing in front of people before Lionel Hampton?

I was working with a couple of tap dancers. I remember the names: Lem Neal and Dickie Sims. They were a team. They picked me up at the theater in my home and asked me, did I want to valet for them? Oh yeah. Anxious to be around show business. This would give me a chance to hear all kind of music. I’m going around, meeting all these guys. I was working with them, and Lester was in the band that was playing on this gig they did.
Lester Young.

Lester Young. He was playing his tenor in the band. He was another one I had fallen in love with – music – it was like hearing birds or somebody. He was in the band. They played. One of the fellows that I worked for said, “Come on, man. They want you to sing.” I said, “What? Want me to sing?” I didn’t know anything about me. I felt like, hey, you know. Anyway, Talk of the Town was the song I sang. [Scott sings:] “I can’t show my face. Can’t go any place. People stop and stare. It’s so hard to bear. Everybody knows I love you. It’s the talk of the town. Friends and our relations send congratulations. I’m not setting our wedding day. Friends and our relations send congratulations. How can I face them? What can I say?” It stops there with me. Those are the last lyrics I remember. But that’s an old song. Talk of the Town.
So you went out and you sang.
I went out and sang that for them. Then they wanted another one. They kept applauding. “Bring him back here. Bring him back here. Give us another.” I could hear

the people say that. It was in Pennsylvania that this was happening. What was that town? I’m trying to think of the town. Not Meadville, but we were near Meadville. You could just cross the street almost and be in Meadville, but this sound started with an S.
Scranton?
Huh?
I forgot. Not Scranton?
No.
So you’re in Pennsylvania . . .
It was little. One of those little towns, little country towns.
So they asked you to do another song after Talk of the Town.
And I did Don’t take your love from me. That was the other one that I did. That and . . .
Talk of the Town.

Yeah, Talk of the Town. Those two I did. That spurred me on. I had done two. Okay, I’m going back home and be a singer. It was a couple of clubs that I knew wanted me to sing for them, but the guy was so cheap, a lot of artists wouldn’t work for it.
So you wouldn’t work with the guy because he was too cheap.

Anyway, I went ahead – like I said, did those two nights with them. They had – this was a weekend – three-night gig that we were on. The dancers had – it was their date. Like I said, it opened my eyes that I could keep on singing.

Yeah. You got the bug. Let me ask you one thing before we leave the initial time you sang Don’t take your love from me and Talk of the Town. When Lester Young said, let him sing, and after you did sing, what was his remarks to you.

He said, “Go back in the dressing room. You’re a valet. You don’t belong out here.” I felt so bad about what he had said to me. So I went back in the dressing room. I didn’t say anything. Just moseyed back in and sat down and thought about it. I said, I don’t have to be insulted like this. I told the fellows. I said, “I’m sorry. I’m going back
home” – the fellows I was working for. So they gave me my money and my fare back home, because I had to take a bus from there to Cleveland. I took the bus fare and got the bus.
